name: Opportunity (MER-B)
short_status: Landed in Eagle crater on 25 January 2004 for a 90-sol mission and worked 5,111 sols, driving 45.16 km. A planet-encircling dust storm ended it: last signal 10 June 2018, mission complete 13 February 2019.
tagline: NASA · United States · Rover · 2004 · The long occupation Ended
stats: sols worked, against a design life of 90 sols
driven, the off-Earth distance record until Perseverance passed it on 11 October 2026
replies to over a thousand commands sent after the storm

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 8 July 2003 at 03:18:15 UT, which was 11:18:15 p.m. EDT on 7 July at the Cape, on a heavy Delta II 7925H from Cape Canaveral. NASA's mission page prints the same instant as 7 July 2003, 20:18:15 PDT, and lists the vehicle as Delta 7925H no. D299 from SLC-17B.

facts.label: Landing
facts.value: 25 January 2004. NSSDCA times touchdown at 04:54:22.7 UT at Mars and 05:05:26.6 UT Earth-received, about 1:15 p.m. local solar time. Entry mass was 827 kg at 19,300 km/h; the aeroshell braked for about four minutes to 1,600 km/h, the parachute took it to roughly 300 km/h, retrorockets and airbags fired from about 100 m, and the bundle struck at around 50 km/h, bounced and rolled to a stop inside a 20 m crater. NASA's own end-of-mission release dates the landing to 24 January 2004 because it was still the 24th in Pacific time at JPL when the signal arrived.

facts.label: Landing site
facts.value: Eagle crater, Meridiani Planum, at 1.946 S and 354.473 E in IAU 2000 body-centred coordinates. NSSDCA describes the landing ellipse as centred at 2.07 S, 353.52 and roughly 119 by 17 km oriented at 88 degrees, although it prints that longitude as west, which cannot be reconciled with the east-positive touchdown figure on the same page. NASA's mission page separately says the rover came down about 9 miles (14.9 km) from its target.

facts.label: The rover itself
facts.value: Six wheels on a rocker-bogie suspension, solar arrays giving up to 140 W in full sun, 128 MB of RAM, and the Athena payload: panoramic camera, Miniature Thermal Emission Spectrometer, Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometer, Moessbauer spectrometer, Microscopic Imager and Rock Abrasion Tool, plus navigation and hazard cameras and a magnet array. NASA's own figures for the rover's mass differ: NSSDCA's Facts in Brief and NASA's mission page list 185 kg, while the 2019 end-of-mission release describes a 384-pound (174-kilogram) rover. The rest of the stack is not disputed: lander platform 348 kg, backshell and parachute 209 kg, heat shield 78 kg, cruise stage 193 kg and 50 kg of propellant, which with the 185 kg rover sums to 1,063 kg off the pad. NSSDCA's own figures do not fully reconcile: those four flight components add to 820 kg against the 827 kg entry mass printed on the same page.

facts.label: Endurance crater
facts.value: JPL's overview caption records Opportunity dipping into Endurance on its 130th sol, 5 June 2004, and getting close to the dunes on its floor by sol 205, 21 August 2004. The crater is described only as football-field-sized; no diameter in metres is given on that page.

facts.label: Design life, and a disputed driving requirement
facts.value: 90 sols. The distance requirement is quoted two different ways by NASA itself. The requirements set out in the mission's own 2003 overview paper include driving at least 600 m, the figure NASA's mission page still gives for the nominal mission; the 2019 end-of-mission release instead says the rover was 'designed to last just 90 Martian days and travel 1,100 yards (1,000 meters)'. The first is a capability floor written before flight, the second a round number written fifteen years later.

facts.label: Total distance
facts.value: 28.06 miles (45.16 km), the figure NASA gives for final odometry when the mission was declared complete on 13 February 2019. The end-of-mission press release itself rounds this to 'more than 28 miles (45 kilometers)'.

facts.label: Off-Earth driving record in 2026
facts.value: Perseverance passed it on 11 October 2026, its sol 2006, when a 91.31 m drive took its odometer to 28.10 miles (45.22 km). JPL announced the new record the next day, and NASA's Mars 2020 traverse file, last modified 15 October 2026, puts the end of that drive at 45,217.391 m. JPL also notes that Perseverance covered in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15.

facts.label: How the record was claimed, and the Lunokhod problem
facts.value: NASA announced on 28 July 2014 that Opportunity had taken the off-world driving record the previous day at 25.01 miles (40.25 km), using 24.2 miles (39 km) for the Soviet Lunokhod 2, a figure the release credits to recent calculations from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images of Lunokhod 2's tracks. That 39 km is not the only published number. Emily Lakdawalla set out the alternatives for the Planetary Society on 21 June 2013, more than a year before the NASA announcement: about 37 km derived from Lunokhod 2's wheel rotations and a low-resolution route map, and about 42 km from a Russian remapping of its actual tracks in the same orbiter's imagery. Opportunity's final 45.16 km clears every one of those figures; the 2014 announcement, measured against the highest of them, was premature.

facts.label: Water at Meridiani
facts.value: Announced 2 March 2004, five weeks after landing. The Moessbauer spectrometer found jarosite, a hydrated iron sulfate; the outcrop was rich in sulfur; it held BB-sized spherules, the objects nicknamed blueberries, later found to be hematite-rich concretions; and it showed cross-bedding. Steve Squyres: 'Liquid water once flowed through these rocks. It changed their texture, and it changed their chemistry.'

facts.label: First meteorite found on another planet
facts.value: In January 2005, near its discarded heat shield, Opportunity found a basketball-sized iron-nickel object that JPL's release of 19 January 2005 called 'the first meteorite of any type ever identified on another planet'. Squyres: 'I never thought we would get to use our instruments on a rock from someplace other than Mars.'

facts.label: Endeavour crater
facts.value: Opportunity reached Endeavour's rim at a spot named Spirit Point on 9 August 2011, after roughly 21 km and nearly three years of driving from Victoria. The USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature places Endeavour at 2.28 S, 354.80 E with a diameter of 21.78 km; the JPL arrival release rounds it to 14 miles (22 km). It was the oldest terrain the rover ever touched, and the last.

facts.label: Homestake
facts.value: A vein of calcium sulfate, 1 to 2 cm wide and 40 to 50 cm long, examined in November 2011 in a zone where the sulfate-rich sedimentary bedrock of the plains meets the older volcanic bedrock exposed at Endeavour's rim, and announced on 7 December 2011. JPL calls it apparently gypsum. Squyres: 'This tells a slam-dunk story that water flowed through underground fractures in the rock.'

facts.label: The storm that ended it
facts.value: Atmospheric opacity over Opportunity, tau, was estimated at 10.8 on 10 June 2018. The 2007 storm, which the rover survived, had peaked somewhere above 5.5. Below about 24 volts the rover trips a low-power fault that shuts off everything except the mission clock, which wakes the computer periodically to ask whether there is enough charge to do anything useful.

facts.label: What the recovery campaign needed
facts.value: JPL's August 2018 summary set out the conditions: tau had to drop below 2 before the arrays could recharge; the Deep Space Network listened several times a week during predicted wake-up windows while JPL's radio science group swept a wider frequency band daily; and three fault states were possible, a low-power hibernation, a mission clock fault, and an uploss fault. None of them produced a signal.

facts.label: End of mission
facts.value: The final recovery commands went out on the evening of 12 February 2019 from JPL's Space Flight Operations Facility, through the 70 m Mars Station antenna at Goldstone, and NASA declared the mission complete the next day. Two command counts circulate for the eight-month campaign. NASA's release says 'more than a thousand commands to restore contact'; the Planetary Society's account of the same effort counts over 835 commands transmitted between the June 2018 loss and 12 February 2019. Neither source says how its count was made.

timeline: Launch at 03:18:15 UT on a heavy Delta II 7925H from Cape Canaveral, the second of the two Mars Exploration Rover launches of 2003.

Touchdown at 04:54:22.7 UT, Earth-received 05:05:26.6 UT. The airbag bundle bounces across Meridiani Planum and rolls to a stop inside a crater about 20 m wide, later named Eagle, with a bedrock outcrop in the wall within 10 metres of the rover. Steve Squyres at the press conference: 'We have scored a 300-million-mile, interplanetary hole-in-one and we are actually inside a small impact crater!'
NASA announces jarosite, sulfates, BB-sized spherules and cross-bedding in the Eagle outcrop: the rocks were once soaked in liquid water.
Endurance crater. NASA's farewell image caption records Opportunity climbing out on sol 315, 12 December 2004, after just over six months inside a stadium-sized hole reading the layers in its walls.

A rehearsal for the end. Dust drops Opportunity's daily power from about 700 watt-hours to 148 on 17 July and 128 on 18 July, and JPL suspends communications to conserve the batteries. Alan Stern, then head of NASA's Science Mission Directorate: 'We're rooting for our rovers to survive these storms, but they were never designed for conditions this intense.'

Victoria crater, about 800 m across and deeper than anything Opportunity had entered before. The rover drives in at Duck Bay and, eleven months later, is sent back up the slope. Rover mission manager Bill Nelson, as the climb-out began: 'If Opportunity were driving with only five wheels, like Spirit, it probably would never get out of Victoria Crater.'
Arrival at Endeavour's rim at Spirit Point, named for its twin, after roughly 21 km and nearly three years of open-country driving from Victoria.
JPL reports that the rover is working in no-flash mode after repeated resets and amnesia events, storing each sol's data in volatile RAM and downlinking it before the rover sleeps.
On sol 3968 a 46.5 m drive takes the odometer to 26.221 miles (42.198 km), past the 26.219 mile Olympic marathon distance, eleven years and two months after landing.

A dust storm that began around 30 May, first flagged to the Opportunity team by the Mars Color Imager on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, grows until by 12 June it covers 14 million square miles (35 million square kilometres), roughly a quarter of Mars.

Sol 5,111. The last downlink from Opportunity reaches Earth, with tau over the rover estimated at 10.8. It is also the last day of a 354-frame panorama begun on sol 5,084; a few frames in the bottom left were never filled in with the green and violet filters.

After a final set of commands sent the previous evening through the 70 m Goldstone antenna, NASA declares the mission complete. Project manager John Callas: 'We have made every reasonable engineering effort to try to recover Opportunity and have determined that the likelihood of receiving a signal is far too low to continue recovery efforts.'
Perseverance passes Opportunity's 45.16 km on its sol 2006, with a 91.31 m drive that takes its odometer to 45.22 km. JPL announces the new off-Earth driving record the next day.

images.caption: PIA17759, a vertical-projection Pancam self-portrait assembled from frames taken 3 to 6 January 2014, about three weeks before Opportunity completed ten years on Mars, with dust still coating the solar arrays after a partial wind cleaning.

PIA05755, the Lion King panorama: an approximate true-colour Pancam mosaic of 558 frames taken on sols 58 and 60 showing Eagle crater, the discarded lander, the bedrock outcrop in the crater wall, and the plains of Meridiani Planum beyond.
PIA19113, a microscopic imager close-up taken beside Fram crater on sol 84, 19 April 2004, with colour added from the panoramic camera; the area shown is about 3 centimetres across.

PIA07110, an approximately true-colour Pancam mosaic of Burns Cliff on the inner southeastern wall of Endurance crater, composited from 46 image sets taken over sols 287 to 294, 13 to 20 November 2004.
PIA09104, a Pancam vista of Victoria crater taken from the promontory called Cape Verde, assembled from hundreds of exposures acquired between sols 970 and 991, 16 October to 7 November 2006.

PIA14509, a Pancam mosaic recorded after Opportunity reached the rim of Endeavour crater on 9 August 2011, showing the Spirit Point area of the rim, the small crater Odyssey, and the interior of Endeavour beyond.

PIA22909, the approximately true-colour version of Opportunity's last panorama: 354 Pancam frames taken in Perseverance Valley between sols 5,084 and 5,111, 13 May to 10 June 2018, with a group of frames at lower left that were never filled in through the green and violet filters before the dust storm ended the mission.
